stories.headline: Three Tren de Aragua members sentenced to 20 years in federal prison for Denver kidnapping and torture
stories.summary:
Three men affiliated with the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua were sentenced Monday to 20 years in federal prison for kidnapping and torturing a Venezuelan immigrant in Denver in October 2024. The victim, a construction worker whose roommates discovered he and his father had been police officers in Venezuela, was held at gunpoint, bound, gagged, and tortured over several days while his captors attempted to extort $30,000 from his family.

According to U.S. Attorney Peter McNeilly, the men sent videos of the torture — including strangulation and pistol-whipping — to the victim's wife in Venezuela. After extortion attempts failed, the men contacted alleged TdA leader Brawins Dominique Suarez Villegas, known as 'Chino San Vicente,' who directed them to cut off the victim's pinky finger with pliers to pressure the family into paying.

Denver police conducted a welfare check on Oct. 16, 2024, but did not locate the victim. After the visit, three of the men fled and the victim escaped, going directly to police. The case was initially investigated by Denver police before being transferred to the FBI and the U.S. Attorney's Office.

Suarez Villegas has been separately indicted on RICO charges and is currently in custody in Colombia awaiting extradition. McNeilly said combating TdA in Colorado remains one of his office's top priorities, noting the gang has been designated a foreign terrorist organization.

stories.headline: Two killed in small plane crash near Boulder's Eldorado Canyon after overnight search
stories.summary:
Two people were found dead Monday in the wreckage of a single-engine aircraft that crashed south of Boulder near Eldorado Canyon State Park, ending an overnight search that spanned roughly 90 square miles. The plane had departed Vance Brand Airport in Longmont and sent out an emergency beacon alert late Sunday near Eldorado Springs before disappearing from radar.

A MedEvac helicopter and the Civil Air Patrol spotted the wreckage around 10:15 a.m. Monday north of Eldorado Canyon State Park and south of the Flatirons in what authorities described as difficult terrain. Rescuers reached the site around noon and confirmed no survivors.

The Boulder County Sheriff's Office and the National Transportation Safety Board are leading the investigation, with an NTSB team expected on site by Tuesday. The Boulder County Coroner's Office is conducting a parallel investigation to determine cause and manner of death, with victim identities pending next-of-kin notification.

stories.headline: Denver Water issues $30,000 in fines, 2,000 warnings as drought-year conservation falls short of 20% goal
stories.summary:
Denver Water customers have reduced their water use by 9% through the end of September, falling well short of the utility's 20% conservation goal set in response to record-breaking drought. The utility received more than 7,500 reports of watering violations over the summer, issuing 2,000 warnings and levying 110 fines totaling approximately $30,000.

The utility's demand planning manager, Greg Fisher, said customers became increasingly responsive as the season progressed — reducing use by just 4% in June but by 14% in both August and September. In total, customers used 10,800 acre-feet less water than normal, enough to supply roughly 54,000 households for a year.

Denver Water implemented mandatory watering restrictions in March — the first since 2013 — limiting customers to twice-weekly watering and imposing tiered billing rates. A full lawn watering ban took effect last Thursday, accompanied by warnings of steeper fines and potential water service shutoffs for violators.

Denver Water serves 1.5 million customers, roughly a quarter of Colorado's population. Fisher said the full ban is expected to accelerate conservation efforts through the end of the warm season.

stories.headline: U.S. Supreme Court appears divided over Boulder County's climate lawsuit against oil companies
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court heard oral arguments Monday in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, a case that will determine whether Boulder County's lawsuit seeking to hold oil companies financially responsible for climate change-related damages can proceed. Justices appeared split, expressing reservations about arguments on both sides.

Boulder County, which filed suit in 2018, claims Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil knowingly deceived consumers about the climate risks of fossil fuels, causing buyers to use more fuel than they otherwise would have. The county wants the companies to pay for floods, wildfires, drought, and building damage attributed to climate change.

The companies and the Justice Department argued that federal law preempts the lawsuit and that allowing it to proceed would effectively let juries in courtrooms across the country set national and international energy policy. An attorney for the companies noted that approximately 90,000 municipalities could bring similar suits if Boulder's claims are allowed to go forward.

The outcome is expected to have broad implications for dozens of similar climate liability lawsuits filed by cities and counties across the country against fossil fuel producers.

stories.headline: Denver City Council's four ballot questions explained ahead of November vote
stories.summary:
Denver voters will decide four city charter amendments in November, placed on the ballot by the City Council and covering topics ranging from wage enforcement to changes in city budgeting and the Civil Service Commission. The measures appear alongside a citizen initiative on foie gras and a Denver Public Schools mill levy override.

Question 2H would formally enshrine wage enforcement — including minimum wage investigations — in the City Auditor's Office charter duties, elevating a responsibility the office has carried informally since 2016. Question 2I would allow the city to adopt a two-year budget planning process and require automatic spending reductions if revenues fall short by 2% or more, at an estimated one-time cost of $50,000.

Question 2J would modernize the Civil Service Commission and Department of Safety by adding gender-neutral language, removing a citizenship requirement for commission members, and updating disciplinary review timelines. A fourth measure, Question 2K, was also approved by the council for the November ballot.

All four questions were approved by the council over the summer. Questions 2H and 2J passed unanimously; Question 2I passed 9-2, with council members Kevin Flynn and Flor Alvidrez voting against.

stories.headline: Alterra Mountain Co. names Kelly Vohs as new CEO ahead of ski season
stories.summary:
Denver-based Alterra Mountain Co., owner of the Ikon Pass and operator of ski resorts across North America, has hired Kelly Vohs as its new chief executive officer. Vohs replaces Jared Smith, who stepped down from the role.

The leadership change comes as Alterra heads into a new ski season following a period of uncertainty over Epic and Ikon pass sales. The company, which owns or operates more than 15 mountain destinations including Steamboat Springs in Colorado and Mammoth Mountain in California, is one of the largest ski resort operators in the world.

The timing of the CEO transition, announced ahead of the winter 2026-27 season, signals a significant strategic moment for the company as it works to recover from what analysts have described as a difficult prior season due to poor snowfall conditions across the West.

stories.headline: Denver temperatures near record highs this week as October heat wave grips Front Range
stories.summary:
Denver and the broader Front Range are experiencing an unseasonably warm stretch of weather, with temperatures forecast to run 10 to 20 degrees above normal through Saturday. Afternoon highs in Denver were expected to approach 88 degrees Monday, potentially breaking the city's October 5 daily record of 87 degrees set in 2024.

The National Weather Service issued a moderate heat risk advisory for Monday, urging caution for heat-sensitive individuals, those without cooling, and some industries and health systems. Cities along the northern Front Range including Fort Collins and Greeley were also flirting with 90-degree temperatures.

The warm spell follows Denver's fourth-warmest September on record — the sixth consecutive September without snowfall in the city. A cooler shift is expected by the weekend.

stories.headline: CDOT begins $1.9 million project to add lane on northbound I-225 in Denver's Hampden South
stories.summary:
The Colorado Department of Transportation has launched a $1.9 million construction project to add a lane to northbound Interstate 225 in south Denver's Hampden South neighborhood. The project will create four continuous through lanes on northbound I-225 between I-25 and South Yosemite Street, addressing a bottleneck caused by drivers merging from I-25.

In addition to the new lane, crews will resurface the roadway and improve drainage infrastructure to help prevent flooding. Construction is expected to continue through December, with both nighttime work (9:30 p.m. to 5:30 a.m., Sunday through Thursday) and daytime work (7 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday).

CDOT does not anticipate major delays but advises drivers to plan for approximately 10 additional minutes of travel time. Intermittent shoulder and ramp closures are expected throughout the project, with updated lane closure information available at COtrip.org.

stories.headline: Update: Broncos avoid worst-case scenarios as Surtain, Bryant, Moss injuries not considered serious
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos received encouraging injury news Monday after all three players who left Sunday's 24-14 loss to the San Francisco 49ers with injuries are expected to avoid season-ending setbacks, sources told The Denver Post. All-Pro cornerback Pat Surtain II and wide receiver Pat Bryant both sustained ankle injuries and are expected to miss games but return this season; neither suffered an Achilles injury.

Cornerback Riley Moss, who left at halftime with a rib injury, is also not considered to have a serious injury, though the extent of his absence is unclear. Head coach Sean Payton declined to update the players' statuses on his Monday conference call with reporters, saying the team would release an injury report Wednesday.

Surtain, 26, went down in visible pain in the final minutes of the first half and needed assistance off the field. Bryant, 23, required a cart to the locker room after being tackled awkwardly on a 31-yard reception in the second half. With Surtain and Moss potentially sidelined, cornerbacks Jahdae Barron and Kris Abrams-Draine are expected to start Sunday against the Los Angeles Chargers.

stories.headline: Broncos' offensive struggles deepen questions about coordinator Davis Webb's future after 2-2 start
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos' 24-14 loss to San Francisco dropped them to 2-2 and intensified scrutiny of offensive coordinator Davis Webb's play-calling after the unit generated just three points in the first three quarters. Denver is averaging 18.5 points per game and ranks in the 20s or worse across a broad range of offensive statistical categories through four weeks.

Head coach Sean Payton, when asked Monday whether he would consider taking the play sheet from the 31-year-old Webb, did not rule it out, saying only that it was 'too early' and that the team 'always looks at everything.' The non-denial drew attention as a signal that Payton may be weighing significant changes to the offense.

Quarterback Bo Nix completed just one pass beyond 10 yards in Sunday's game, according to passing chart data. Running back RJ Harvey continued to show value as a receiver with 10 catches for 68 yards, but the overall offense struggled to generate explosive plays or force opposing defenses out of soft coverage schemes.

Denver hosts the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 5 on Sunday.

stories.headline: Denver Pioneers open college hockey season ranked No. 1 after sweeping Alaska Anchorage
stories.summary:
The University of Denver men's hockey team retained the No. 1 ranking in the USA Hockey poll released Monday after sweeping Alaska Anchorage to open the 2026-27 season. The Pioneers won 6-2 and 4-1 in the two-game series.

Freshman Daxon Rudolph led DU with five points across the two games, while sophomore Kristian Epperson added three points. Sam Harris and Jake Harris each scored two goals in the series.

Denver will host the USA Hockey Under-18 team at 6 p.m. Saturday before a marquee home series against No. 2 Michigan on Oct. 16 and 17.

stories.headline: New steakhouse opens in Littleton; Mile High United Way hires new communications chief; Western wear retailer coming to Colorado Mills
stories.summary:
Summit Steak Bar has opened at 5869 Alkire St. in Littleton, featuring an in-house beef cutting and dry-aging program. The restaurant is owned by husband-and-wife team George and Tammy Pesek; chef-owner George Pesek, an accomplished mountaineer who has completed the Seven Summits, inspired the establishment's name. The venue also includes a members-only speakeasy called the High Steaks Club, accessible via a $500 coin with limited availability.

Mile High United Way announced the hiring of Megan McRae as its new chief communications officer. McRae, a longtime Denver journalist who most recently served as senior news director at Denver7-KMGN and previously held a similar role at 9NEWS, had served on Mile High United Way's Board of Trustees from 2024 to 2026.

Cavender's Boot City is scheduled to open Friday at Colorado Mills in Lakewood, marking the Western wear retailer's fourth Colorado location. The 15,016-square-foot store at 14500 W. Colfax Ave. will carry boots, hats, jeans, dresses, and accessories from brands including Ariat, Wrangler, and Resistol.

topStory.headline: Trump Suggests Iran Could 'Take Out' Los Angeles and San Diego, Drawing Condemnation from California Officials
topStory.summary:
President Donald Trump told supporters at a campaign rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday night that Iran could be allowed to destroy Los Angeles and San Diego, framing potential attacks on two of America's largest cities as an acceptable cost of the ongoing U.S. war with Iran. 'They can take out a city,' Trump said. 'Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.' The crowd applauded. Trump added that the conflict 'will end very quickly, one way or the other, very soon.'

The remarks drew immediate and sharp condemnation from California's governor and the mayors of both cities. Governor Gavin Newsom wrote on X that Trump was 'deranged and dangerous,' noting that the president had already deployed the National Guard and Marines to California. 'The President is advocating for an attack on 10+ million U.S. residents in two of America's largest cities,' Newsom said in a follow-up statement from his press office. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said it was the president's role 'to protect the country, not to actively threaten it,' while San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that his city was 'not collateral damage' and 'never a small price to pay.'

The comments were made during a wide-ranging speech of nearly an hour and a half in which Trump also argued that economic pressures caused by the Iran war were a 'small price to pay for keeping the world safe.' It was not immediately clear whether Trump was making a crude rhetorical point about liberal-leaning cities, or whether he was referencing actual intelligence about Iranian targeting capabilities. Some conservative commentators argued Trump was speaking about high gas prices rather than literal military strikes. The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The strategic significance of both cities adds weight to the controversy. San Diego is home to major U.S. military installations, making it a critical node in American defense infrastructure. Los Angeles hosts the U.S. Space Force's Space Systems Command Headquarters, major aerospace contractors including Lockheed Martin, Boeing, and Northrop Grumman, and federally funded research centers such as the RAND Corporation. U.S. defense officials have previously stated that Iran does not currently possess the capability to launch a direct missile strike on the American mainland.

The episode deepens an already contentious relationship between the Trump administration and California, a state that has been a repeated target of federal actions during Trump's presidency. With November midterm elections approaching, Trump had framed the Nebraska rally in part around building political momentum. The remarks are likely to intensify scrutiny of the administration's handling of the Iran conflict and its rhetoric toward Democratic-led states.
